title: Analysis of polarization drift of optical signals over deployed aerial-inground fiber connections
authors: Aneesh Ramaswamy, Nageswara S. V. Rao, Joseph C. Chapman, Muneer Alshowkan
abstract: Polarization measurements of a classical 1550-nm signal are collected and analyzed on 15-km hybrid aerial-inground fiber connections over 11 months. The spectral area and spectral moments9 of mHz-resolution Fast-Fourier-Transform (FFT) of these measurements are extracted, and related to temperature, humidity, wind speed, and time of day. Spectral area correlations show a strong11 diurnal structure: daytime maxima align with temperatures/wind speed peaks and humidity dips, with lower levels during the night. These diurnal patterns also show seasonality, with higher13 mean and variance in summer than winter. A random forest regressor is used to estimate FFT features from environmental measurements, informed by a theoretical model
summary: This research analyzes polarization drift in long-haul optical fibers by correlating high-resolution spectral features extracted from 1550-nm signals with environmental data like temperature and humidity. By combining extensive field measurements, machine learning regression, and advanced theoretical modeling of birefringence accumulation, the authors provide a robust framework for predicting link degradation, which is critical for deploying quantum communication networks.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is polarization drift of optical signals over deployed aerial-inground fiber connections, which severely degrades the performance and fidelity of quantum communication links.
main_result: The study established strong diurnal and seasonal correlations between measurable spectral features (like spectral area) and environmental factors ($T$, $H$, $W$), providing a framework for weather-aware prediction of polarization drift. The theoretical work also provided explicit mathematical tools using BCH formulas to model drift accumulation across fiber segments.
method: The approach combines extensive field measurements analyzed via Fast-Fourier Transform (FFT) feature extraction with advanced statistical modeling, including Random Forest regression and Principal Component Analysis (PCA), alongside rigorous theoretical derivations using stochastic differential equations and the Magnus expansion.
model_or_system: The system is a 15-km hybrid aerial-inground fiber connection transmitting a classical 1550-nm signal used to characterize quantum link quality. The underlying physics models polarization drift as unitary rotations governed by birefringence ($\zeta_t$), which depends on temperature and mechanical stress.
key_observables: Spectral area, spectral centroid, spectral variance, spectral entropy, $ eta$-exponent of the power spectrum, entanglement throughput, and fidelity.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), relative humidity ($H$), wind speed ($W$), 15-km link length, and measurement time scales (diurnal/seasonal variations).
main_assumptions: Assumptions include negligible Polarization Dependent Loss (PDL) and the use of stochastic treatments to manage multi-segment complexity in the theoretical modeling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the measurement setup, seasonal trends of polarization drift FFT variables correlated with environment, and residual plots showing multiplicative bias in spectral area estimation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from empirical data analysis (measuring spectral features vs. weather) to developing a complex theoretical model for birefringence accumulation across fiber segments using rotation operators, culminating in a predictive framework for quantum link state estimation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of deploying quantum communication networks over real-world infrastructure by quantifying and predicting environmental noise sources affecting polarization states. The combination of advanced signal processing (FFT features) with rigorous fiber optics theory is highly relevant to open quantum systems in noisy environments.
